Toute dénonciation ne vaut que par la so: A call-out is only worth the solution or the change it brings about.
Depuis la mort de George Floyd, les lang: Since the death of George Floyd, people have been speaking out about systemic racism. A #MeTwo — a term used to call out racist attacks and harassment — is unfolding in every field. Even journalists, who are usually bound by a duty of reserve, are coming out of the shadows to denounce the sometimes oppressive climate in their profession. Some, such as <l1>Maya Johnson</l1>, <l2>Christine Genier</l2> and<l3> Denise Balkissoon</l3> in English Canada, have done so with great fanfare. Resignations, open letters, cries from the heart on Twitter: accounts from racialized journalists are increasingly numerous.
Dans les médias francophones et au Québe: In francophone media and in Quebec, people are speaking out more and more too, though more timidly. The journalists we approached for this article had a lot to say, but still feared the repercussions on their careers. We spoke to eight journalists from several major outlets, including Radio-Canada, TVA, Bell Média, CTV and Global News.
<strong>Prioriser sa santé mentale… et s: Putting your mental health first… and your talent
Au fil des témoignages, un thème central: One central theme ran through the testimonies. Every person interviewed spoke, in one way or another, about the mental health toll of racism. “One like you is fine, but no more than that,” a superior once told Oussayma Canbarieh, a documentary filmmaker and journalist. Before going freelance, Oussayma, who is of Syrian origin and wears the hijab, worked for many major media outlets in Quebec. She quickly sensed there were limits to her inclusion.
« C’est subtil : on t’exclut de certaine: “It’s subtle: you’re left out of certain conversations or projects, your name isn’t said, your ideas aren’t considered. Sometimes it’s as simple as a look that says it all…” she explains. For Oussayma, spending her life fighting to carve out a place was out of the question. “Honestly, I admire the people who do it, and it takes a lot, but personally, it drains me too much and it stifles my creativity,” she explains.
Toute cette énergie, je préfère la mettr: “I prefer to put all that energy into my projects and make my place another way.” That is what she did by going freelance, and she considers her career to be going much better since. Better still, she now has the opportunity to offer mentorship and internships to other young journalists from diverse backgrounds. Inevitably, she encourages them to adopt an entrepreneurial mindset. “I often say that if you feel there’s a glass ceiling or that doors are closed, create your own opportunities!
Démarre un projet, crée un réseau », dit: Start a project, build a network,” she says. What’s more, she believes this mindset lets you go further and push past borders. While Oussayma decided to channel her passion into working for herself, other racialized journalists end up leaving their jobs or even the field altogether.
Elena* is a young Black journalist. For her, the problem starts as early as school. In her cohort, she was one of the few racialized people. “My contributions were always a bit different, my ideas and my questions clashed or created discomfort. It ends up making you question your relevance or even your intelligence,” she recounts.
À un certain point, elle s’est même dema: At one point, she even wondered whether she belonged in the journalism program, one that, in her eyes, offered no different perspectives. “We learned to write and take photos, but not to think about the meaning of journalism and its human and societal impact,” she laments. “I even wondered whether I should drop out. I felt different, isolated. But I told myself that maybe it’s when you’re isolated that your voice matters most.”
À peine sortie de l’université, après qu: Barely out of university, after a few internships, she landed at Radio-Canada. A dream job for many beginning journalists. But Elena was quickly disillusioned. On a regular basis, she put up with “jokes, questionable questions and other microaggressions.” For example, when the team had to cover the crash of Iranian flight PS-752 last January, which killed Canadians, a colleague made contemptuous comments about Iran, implying that, in any case, the people who travelled there were “asking for trouble.”
À une autre occasion, après avoir manife: On another occasion, after she expressed interest in an internal promotion, another colleague threw at her: “Yeah, sure, you’ll get it because you’re Black!” Whether or not she was the target, each of these inappropriate exchanges deepened her discomfort. Sometimes, it was her work itself that was called into question.
« Un chef de pupitre d’une autre région: “An assignment editor from another region of the country once called me and argued with me for 30 minutes to get me to change the term ‘racialized’ in one of my pieces. He said it was a political, disturbing term,” she says. She remembers clearly feeling suffocated at that moment and telling herself she wouldn’t be able to stand such a work environment for long. After a year, Elena chose to leave Radio-Canada. “To tell you the truth, I don’t want to work with Quebec media anymore,” she says under her breath. “Some people have the energy to fight, but others think about their mental health and resign.
Les médias sont en train de perdre des g: The media are losing talented people. I tell myself that all the energy I put into fighting to exist, I could use to produce quality reports and give a voice to underrepresented communities,” says the young journalist, who now works for an English-language outlet in Ontario, where she feels more listened to. “I feel like I can contribute more in English-language media,” she confides. For Elena, the duty of reserve is also sometimes a way of silencing voices that disturb. “It’s easy to talk about neutrality when your life isn’t in danger. I’m a Black journalist, my perspective is necessarily different when we talk about fundamental rights.” She notes radio silence from francophone racialized journalists when it comes to denouncing racism.
« Je pense que la culture francophone es: “I think francophone culture is very violent toward racialized people. There’s always a fight of the oppressed people.” The journalist believes there is a form of violence in the denial of racism, which keeps racialized people from feeling confident enough to denounce racism in francophone media. Today, media here and elsewhere are more inclined to want to include these different voices and perspectives. Some even make an effort to make room for diversity in all its forms. “Yes, they want the voices, but how do they treat the individuals behind those voices? That’s the question we need to ask ourselves,” concludes Elena.
Si Elena est restée dans le domaine, d’a: While Elena stayed in the field, others have left it. Nadim Moghrabi, who is of Lebanese origin, worked at Radio-Canada in Montréal and Toronto more than 20 years ago. The two experiences were completely different for him.
À Toronto, il a travaillé pendant quatre: In Toronto, he worked for four years as a journalist for several outlets, including Radio-Canada. During those four years, he contributed to several cultural programs. He loved his experience and felt accepted for who he was, entirely. He then left Toronto to return to Montréal. On his return, he was offered an internship as a researcher. “My time at Radio-Canada Montréal lasted three months, before I got completely fed up,” he recounts.
J’ai senti qu’on ne me faisait pas confi: I felt they didn’t trust me, that they were throwing all kinds of obstacles in my way. I wasn’t given the means to grow, it wasn’t an enriching experience.” It has now been 20 years since he left the media world to work in insurance, and he feels that nothing has changed since.
Cette notion du politique revient souven: This notion of what counts as “political” comes up often for racialized journalists. Everyone interviewed for this article believes that the duty of neutrality, or the concept of objectivity in journalism, often favours white people and applies a double standard. During the years Pascale* spent in a major newsroom, this feeling of exclusion affected her work. “I wasn’t allowed to make mistakes. The expectations for my work were much higher than for everyone else’s.
C’était épuisant », se souvient-elle. Pl: It was exhausting,” she remembers. What’s more, she quickly realized that people were knowingly avoiding offering her opportunities or topics for which she was perfectly qualified. “When it’s a subject that affects my community, for example, suddenly I become relevant to my team. Suddenly, I have value: they want my contacts, my perspective… but not to put me in front of the camera.”
La goutte qui a fait déborder le vase, p: The last straw for her was the treatment she received when she returned from maternity leave. “I felt like a number, an object. And I promised myself it was the last time a white man would make me cry.” Pascale remembers her discomfort during the public debate on blackface. “I felt stress, the weight of that famous objectivity,” she admits. “I felt suffocated, I needed to channel that energy. I started a personal project on the side, where I could interview whoever I wanted and give a voice to different people. It felt good.”
Aujourd’hui, elle constate que les langu: Today, she sees people speaking out more. “Many racialized or Indigenous people are bound by a duty of reserve. Not only journalists, but also executives, for example. But the boldness of activists who have nothing to lose and the context of the American movement give them more courage.” Today, she works in a completely different field.
« Je n’avais aucun espoir de monter plus: “I had no hope of moving up, of fulfilling my ambitions. But I didn’t want to leave and have the newsroom with no racialized people. Eventually, a second Black journalist arrived, and I felt relief. I resigned for my mental health,” she admits simply.
<strong>Trop de non-blancs dans son trav: Too many non-white people in her work
Ailleurs au Canada, les dénonciations su: Elsewhere in Canada, call-outs are pouring in on Twitter. But they often come from established journalists. How do racialized journalists at the start of their careers experience the industry? Zora decided to become a journalist in order to change perspectives. Her first paid job in the industry was a researcher position at CTV Toronto. She wanted to highlight the voices of racialized people. A motivation she says she made clear to the team when she was hired.
« On m’a dit que ma voix était important: “I was told my voice was important, while the other racialized people in the newsroom were referred to as ‘diversity hires,’” she says. But Zora’s experience lasted only six weeks, and she believes racism was the cause. Her contract ended while she was in training for another position within the company. “I was making an extra effort not to always have white guests on our panels,” she confides. “A senior employee then told me there were too many non-white people among my guests and that I talked a lot about racial issues.” Another racialized journalist who worked at CTV, who prefers to remain anonymous, corroborates this comment.
« Un collègue blanc m’a fait la remarque: “A white colleague remarked that there were too many racialized people among the guests I was choosing,” says the young journalist. According to Zora, the senior CTV employee also made remarks about her clothing, telling her she was “too modest.” He also reportedly told her he was disappointed she wasn’t of Latina origin, but Arab instead.
« Il m’a dit que ça serait mieux si j’ét: “He told me it would be better if I were Latina,” she adds. Zora says she heard several Islamophobic, homophobic and racist remarks in the Toronto newsroom. “I once heard an employee describe a South Asian host as ‘the brown woman’ and say directly to her, ‘O.K., brown lady,’ when we were discussing diversity.”
Un climat qu’a également vécu le second: A climate also experienced by the second CTV journalist we interviewed, who prefers not to be named. “They made jokes about the appearance of a Black guest who wore locs, implying he looked like he was on drugs. I remember another time when a Black colleague who had just been promoted was described as ‘another Black person taking over,’” he recounts. Neither employee told human resources about their experiences for fear of reprisals. Today, young Zora tells us in tears how her work to promote diversity was met with resistance.
« Je sais que ces salles de presse ne so: “I know these newsrooms aren’t safe for people like us. Many of the racialized journalists who break through in the industry conform to whiteness. They don’t question systems of power. I didn’t walk into CTV intending to conform to whiteness. I feel that despite all my efforts, nobody cared whether I was doing my job well or not; I was disruptive.”
La Converse a tenté de discuter avec la: La Converse tried to speak with CTV’s general manager, Lis Travers, who had been in contact with Zora. She did not respond to our requests and forwarded our email to the director of communications, Emilie Young Lee, who asked for clarification. When we explained the reason for our requests and the alleged facts, she did not respond to our requests sent on June 11. After a follow-up on June 16, we still have not received a reply from her.
Nous avons également communiqué avec l’e: We also contacted the senior employee named in some of these allegations so that he could confirm or deny them. He instead directed us to CTV communications. In an emailed statement, CTV’s vice-president of communications, Scott Henderson, would not confirm or deny the allegations of the company’s two former junior journalists. “We do not discuss matters relating to our employees, it is an institutional policy. However, we take these issues seriously. Bell is committed to building a diverse and collaborative workplace, and we have taken a stand against racism,” CTV said.
Et le rôle des alliés, dans tout ça ? Il: And what about the role of allies in all this? It is crucial, reminds Oussayma Canbarieh. “We must not forget that without allies in positions of power who give us a chance or push us to go further, it would be hard to make a place for ourselves.”
Mais ce rôle n’est pas toujours de tout: But this role isn’t always easy. Dominique Charron also had to leave a web editor position at Espaces autochtones in 2017, to escape a climate she considered toxic. As an ally and a white woman, she too felt suffocated by the climate in Quebec media. The events of recent months inspired her to speak out. Once again, the inappropriate comments were always at the edge of social acceptability, somewhere between a wink and a laugh, she says. “I remember a colleague who had gone to report in a Mohawk community. When she came back, a desk editor said to her, ‘Ah, the Mohawks didn’t keep you?’ (insinuating a violent nature).
Je n’en étais pas revenue », se remémore: I couldn’t believe it,” she recalls. For Dominique Charron, it was inconceivable to work in such an outlet without understanding the role of an Indigenous media organization and without trying to build real ties with communities. “I sensed the underlying lack of empathy. It was a fairly superficial approach,” she notes. When she left her position, Dominique wrote to human resources, but also wrote a Facebook post to denounce some of these practices. “I know that a few of my colleagues who reacted positively to my post were sanctioned.”
La Converse a obtenu une copie d’un cour: La Converse obtained a copy of an email from Espaces autochtones management to the supervisors of the Radio-Canada journalists who liked the Facebook post by Dominique. Today, she believes her speaking out is important to move things forward on the question of diversity in the media. “It’s hard and delicate, but it’s by naming things that they will change.”
Questionné au sujet des témoignages de D: Asked about the testimonies of Dominique and Elena*, Radio-Canada’s director of diversity, Luc Simard, indicated by email that he could not comment on these experiences as he was not aware of them. He directed us to director of communications Marc Pichette, who said he takes these allegations seriously and intends to forward them to the relevant management teams.
Concernant le témoignage de Nadim Moghra: Regarding Nadim Moghrabi’s testimony, Radio-Canada declined to comment on the situation in 2000. “CBC/Radio-Canada is firmly committed to fighting racism in all its forms. Racist behaviour or remarks are unacceptable in our workplaces,” Marc Pichette added in his email.
Toute dénonciation ne vaut que par la so: A call-out is only worth the solution or the change it brings about. Elysia Bryan-Baynes, a retired Black journalist from Global Montreal, offers several avenues for reflection. For her, commentators and columnists should be more diverse in the media. “I think that’s where we need to work.
Donner une valeur à l’opinion profession: Giving value to the professional opinion of racialized people, putting them forward, that’s an important step.” She also believes there is a favourable moment to seize right now. “You have to understand who your allies are and not give up. You have as many rights as everyone else, and people increasingly understand that racism is very often subtle, systemic.”
En ce sens, de nombreuses réflexions ont: In that vein, many discussions have begun on how to ensure real inclusion of diversity in traditional media. Last June, a panel organized by the American organization Poynter looked at ways for racialized journalists to raise their voices without losing their jobs. Here are a few:
Trouver un ou des alliés pour dénoncer u: Find one or more allies to denounce a situation as a group.
Ne pas se concentrer sur l’objectivité,: Don’t focus on objectivity, but rather on transparency, accuracy of information and good faith.
Ne pas hésiter à ouvrir la discussion et: Don’t hesitate to open the discussion and talk with people who have a different view.
Tenir son bout devant un rédacteur en ch: Stand your ground with an editor-in-chief or an assignment editor, respectfully and by presenting clear information. If time is short and the journalist has to let go, come back to the subject later to keep it from happening again.
Sur le plan personnel, se souvenir de se: On a personal level, remember your values and ambitions to stay motivated. Use positive affirmations.
Trouver des moyens de canaliser ses émot: Find ways to channel your emotions. This can be through safe spaces or conversations with other racialized journalists.
Évidemment, le poids repose également et: Obviously, the burden also, and above all, rests on editors-in-chief and institutions to dismantle the mechanisms at the source. This has long been acknowledged, discussed, studied. Speaking out publicly will certainly help speed up the process.
